data.name: Fairness can soften unfair rules
data.plainSummary: Sometimes applying a rule word-for-word produces an unfair outcome. Judges and lawmakers should be able to soften rigid rules so real cases line up better with what people mean by justice.
data.whyRoot: Rules are written in advance for typical cases; life produces outliers. Without a safety valve for proportion and fairness, law becomes mechanical cruelty. Equity is a root because justice is not the same as a checklist.
data.description: Foundational claim drawn from Roman jurisprudence that aequitas—fairness and proportion—guides judges and lawmakers in tempering rigid rules so outcomes align with justice in concrete cases.

data.name: You decide what happens to your body
data.plainSummary: Competent adults should generally call the shots about their own bodies, including medical choices, unless there is a strong overriding reason—such as serious harm to others.
data.whyRoot: Your body is the medium through which you experience everything; if others controlled it by default, personal agency would mean little. We take bodily authority as a root because it pairs moral personhood with a zone of decision-making that others must justify crossing.
data.description: Foundational claim that competent adults have primary moral and legal authority over their own bodies, including medical choices, absent overriding harm to others.

data.name: The law should fit together as one clear system
data.plainSummary: Legal rules should fit together into a clear, coherent system—often worked out through careful reasoning and codes—rather than a messy pile of unrelated edicts.
data.whyRoot: People need to know what duties and rights they actually have. If law is a tangle of contradictions, planning and fairness collapse. Coherence is treated as foundational because predictable, unified rules are what let strangers coordinate without constant conflict.
data.description: Foundational civilian ideal that legal rules should form a coherent body, developed through reasoned commentary and (where appropriate) codification, traceable to Roman models of ordered private law and public authority.

data.name: Everyone deserves equal consideration
data.plainSummary: Everyone who counts in the discussion should matter equally when we weigh rights, burdens, and opportunities, unless there is a specific reason to treat people differently.
data.whyRoot: Arbitrary favoritism turns law into club rules. Starting from equal consideration forces reasons for unequal treatment into the open. It is a root because it blocks ‘my group counts more’ as a silent default.
data.description: Foundational claim that all persons (or all in a defined scope) deserve equal standing in moral and often legal reasoning about rights, burdens, and opportunities, absent specific differences that justify unequal treatment.

data.name: When a lot is at stake, follow the evidence
data.plainSummary: When laws or rules seriously affect health, safety, or freedom, they should follow the best available evidence and expert consensus when that exists.
data.whyRoot: When mistakes are costly and reversible only with difficulty, guessing is a poor basis for coercion. Anchoring high-stakes rules to our best shared picture of facts is a root commitment: it reduces arbitrary harm and makes public justification possible.
data.description: Foundational commitment that when laws or regulations materially affect health, safety, or liberty, they should align with credible empirical and expert consensus where such evidence exists.

data.name: Parties owe each other fair dealing
data.plainSummary: In bargains and ongoing legal relationships, each side should treat the other fairly—not only follow the letter of the contract while acting in a one-sided or exploitative way.
data.whyRoot: Bargaining assumes each party can count on something beyond gamesmanship. If only the bare form of words counted, clever abuse would win and cooperation would stay fragile. Fair dealing is a root commitment because it names the minimum mutual respect that makes long-term relationships workable.
data.description: Foundational commitment to reciprocal fairness in performance and enforcement: parties may not weaponize formal rights to surprise, oppress, or take advantage in ways civil-law and common-law systems often capture under abuse-of-right or good-faith doctrines.

data.name: Keep the spirit of your agreements
data.plainSummary: Once you undertake a commitment, you should stand by its purpose and reasonable expectations—not only the narrowest reading that benefits you.
data.whyRoot: Promises coordinate expectations over time. If people could always dodge the point of a deal whenever a loophole appeared, others could not rely on undertakings, and cooperation would stall. Fidelity to the bargain is foundational because it is what makes words actually binding in practice.
data.description: Foundational commitment to loyalty to the bargain (allied with pacta-related ideas in many traditions): performance and interpretation should respect the agreement’s intent and the trust the other party reasonably placed in you.

data.name: Be truthful in agreements and dealings
data.plainSummary: In legal and private relationships, people should tell the truth, avoid misleading others, and disclose what fairness requires—not exploit silence or fine print in bad faith.
data.whyRoot: Voluntary cooperation rests on a shared picture of reality: if people can lie or hide what matters, planning, exchange, and trust break down. We treat honesty as a stopping point because without it, weaker parties are easy to manipulate and almost nothing else in private law can be relied on.
data.description: Foundational commitment that veracity and good-faith disclosure matter in forming, performing, and interpreting obligations; a building block for doctrines of fraud, misrepresentation, and implied duties in many legal systems.

data.name: Freedom first; limits need a good reason
data.plainSummary: People should generally be free to choose for themselves. If you limit someone’s freedom, you owe a real reason—like preventing harm—not just habit or preference.
data.whyRoot: Liberty is costly to restrict and easy to abuse: every constraint needs a public justification. This root flips the burden—freedom is presumed, interference is what must earn its keep—so power cannot treat restriction as the default mood of government.
data.description: Foundational liberal or libertarian commitment that interference with voluntary choice requires a positive justification (harm prevention, consent of the governed, etc.), rather than the reverse.

data.name: Human life matters on its own
data.plainSummary: Human life matters for its own sake—not only because it is useful. Many arguments about ethics and medicine start from this idea.
data.whyRoot: If life only mattered when it was convenient or productive, people could be discarded whenever costs rose. Treating human life as carrying weight on its own is a stopping point for a huge swath of medical and legal reasoning: it says persons are not mere instruments.
data.description: Foundational claim that human life is valuable in itself, often used as a root for autonomy and medical ethics arguments within many frameworks.

data.name: Reduce suffering
data.plainSummary: Morally, we should care about reducing pain and hardship (and often improving well-being) for everyone affected by a decision.
data.whyRoot: Suffering is the clearest signal that something is going wrong for a subject of experience. Many ethical systems stop here because once you admit suffering counts, you have a reason to weigh outcomes and side effects instead of treating people as props in someone else’s story.
data.description: Classical utilitarian starting point: moral weight attaches to the reduction of suffering (and often the promotion of well-being) across those affected.

data.name: Courts should follow their past decisions
data.plainSummary: What courts decided before should usually bind or strongly guide what they decide next, so the law stays predictable—unless there is a compelling reason to change course.
data.whyRoot: Legal disputes are supposed to be settled by rules people could have seen coming. If every case started from scratch, law would be arbitrary and investment in cooperation would shrink. Precedent is a root commitment to stability and notice.
data.description: Foundational commitment that adjudication should be stable and predictable by treating prior court decisions as authoritative or highly persuasive absent compelling reason to depart—core to the Anglo-American common law tradition.

data.name: We shouldn't accept deaths we could prevent
data.plainSummary: If we already know how to prevent a death—through medicine, policy, or basic infrastructure—we should not accept that death without a very strong reason. That stance is common in public health and in longevity-focused worldviews.
data.whyRoot: Once you can prevent harm at reasonable cost, letting it happen anyway usually needs a positive defense—otherwise neglect looks like a choice. This root ties ‘we could have acted’ to moral urgency, not just regret after the fact.
data.description: Foundational commitment that deaths avoidable through known means (medical, policy, or infrastructure) ought not to occur without strong justification; common in public-health and longevity-oriented frameworks.

data.name: A written constitution is the highest law
data.plainSummary: The basic rules of government should be written in a charter that sits above ordinary laws: it divides power, sets up institutions, and limits what legislatures can do.
data.whyRoot: Power needs stable, public limits so people can plan their lives and hold rulers accountable. A supreme written charter is a root in this tradition because it makes those limits visible and harder to erase in a single ordinary vote.
data.description: Foundational commitment that political authority should be structured by a written charter that allocates powers, defines institutions, and stands above ordinary legislation—central to the U.S. federal order.

data.name: Right to access experimental therapy
data.description: A legal concept describing circumstances under which patients may access therapies not yet fully approved under ordinary regulatory pathways.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Depends heavily on jurisdiction-specific statutes and regulatory exceptions.

pros.claim: Can expand options for patients facing serious or life-threatening conditions.
pros.evidence: Expanded access and similar programs exist specifically to address urgent unmet medical need.

cons.claim: May expose patients to interventions with uncertain benefit-risk profiles.
cons.evidence: Early-phase evidence often does not establish efficacy; harm can still occur.

early-phase-evidence-limit.title: Clinical evidence limitations in early-phase trials

data.name: Bodily autonomy
data.description: A derived principle that persons have substantial authority over what happens to their own bodies, including medical decisions.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Widely recognized in medical ethics and law, though boundaries remain contested at the edges.

pros.claim: Aligns with widely accepted informed consent frameworks in clinical practice.
pros.evidence: Informed consent is a standard requirement across modern healthcare systems.

cons.claim: May conflict with public health measures that require mandatory interventions.
cons.evidence: Vaccination mandates and quarantine powers illustrate recurring tension between autonomy and collective welfare.

public-health-tension-note.title: Public health vs. individual autonomy — introductory note

data.name: Good faith (bona fides) in private law
data.plainSummary: Roman private law ties these ideas together: be honest, deal fairly, and keep faith with your agreements—so obligations and interpretation are guided by bona fides, not bare formalism alone.
data.description: Synthesis principle from classical Roman jurisprudence: obligations, interpretation, and conduct in private law should be guided by bona fides—honesty, fair dealing, and loyalty to the bargain—rather than compliance with the letter alone.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Central to civilian systems and influential elsewhere; exact scope and institutional form vary by jurisdiction.

pros.claim: Aligns contract and property law with lived expectations of trust and cooperation.
pros.evidence: Good-faith standards appear across modern civil codes and influence common-law doctrines such as implied duties and unconscionability.

cons.claim: Open-ended good-faith language can create uncertainty about duties and liability.
cons.evidence: Debates over certainty vs. flexibility recur wherever courts imply obligations beyond express terms.

good-faith-uncertainty-note.title: Indeterminacy and good-faith standards — introductory note

data.name: Common law method
data.description: Much of U.S. law (especially in contracts, torts, property, and procedure) develops through judicial decisions that articulate, distinguish, and incrementally reshape rules—alongside statutes and constitutions.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Descriptive of large swaths of state and federal practice, though modern codes and regulations narrow its domain in many fields.

pros.claim: Allows law to adapt flexibly to new facts and evolving norms without waiting for comprehensive legislation.
pros.evidence: Judge-made doctrines continue to govern many private-law disputes and procedural details.

cons.claim: Can obscure clear rules, increase litigation costs, and yield uneven development across jurisdictions.
cons.evidence: Forum variation and complex multi-factor tests are common criticisms in tort and contract doctrine.

jurisdictions.citation: Mixed state and federal court development; no single enactment date

common-law-complexity-critique.title: Complexity and variation in common law doctrines — introductory note

data.name: Constitutional supremacy
data.description: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land; inconsistent statutes and other government acts yield to it (including state law under the Supremacy Clause).
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Expressly stated in Article VI; uniformly treated as bedrock in federal jurisprudence.

pros.claim: Creates a single hierarchy of norms so rights and structural limits are not overridden by ordinary politics alone.
pros.evidence: Judicial invalidation of conflicting enactments is treated as a normal mechanism for enforcing written limits.

cons.claim: Shifts contentious value questions into constitutional interpretation, sometimes amplifying judicial power and social polarization.
cons.evidence: High-stakes disputes often turn on contested readings of open-textured provisions.

art-vi-supremacy.title: U.S. Constitution, Article VI, Clause 2 (Supremacy Clause)

constitutional-polarization-note.title: Constitutional politics and interpretive disagreement — introductory note

data.name: Due process of law
data.description: Government must follow fair procedures—and in substantive strands, respect certain baseline protections—before depriving persons of life, liberty, or property (Fifth Amendment as to federal power; Fourteenth as to states).
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Deeply embedded in federal and state practice; central to modern rights litigation.

pros.claim: Guards against arbitrary punishment, secret proceedings, and capricious administrative action.
pros.evidence: Procedural requirements such as notice and hearing are standard features of deprivation scenarios.

cons.claim: Open-ended phrasing invites wide judicial discretion and disagreement over what process is “due” and what substance is protected.
cons.evidence: Long-running doctrinal splits over incorporation, fundamental rights, and administrative due process.

fifth-fourteenth-due-process.title: U.S. Constitution, Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments (Due Process Clauses)

due-process-open-texture.title: Due process doctrine — variability and debate

data.name: Equal protection of the laws
data.description: States must not deny any person within their jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws—requiring that classifications among persons be justified by standards that vary with the context and the right at stake.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Core Fourteenth Amendment strand driving anti-discrimination and classification review.

pros.claim: Provides a constitutional lever against invidious discrimination and arbitrary class legislation.
pros.evidence: Used to invalidate or strictly scrutinize discriminatory state action across domains.

cons.claim: Tiered scrutiny and malleable standards generate persistent uncertainty and high-stakes judicial balancing.
cons.evidence: Ongoing doctrinal controversy over which groups and interests trigger which level of review.

fourteenth-equal-protection.title: U.S. Constitution, Fourteenth Amendment, Section 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

equal-protection-scrutiny-debate.title: Equal protection tiers of scrutiny — overview

data.name: Federalism (division of sovereign authority)
data.description: Sovereignty is split between a national government and the states: each has distinct lawmaking and enforcement domains, with federal law supreme only within enumerated federal powers.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Structurally embedded in the Constitution’s enumeration of powers and the Tenth Amendment’s reservation to the states.

pros.claim: Allows policy experimentation and local responsiveness while preserving a unified national sphere for certain matters.
pros.evidence: Historical variation among state laws alongside nationwide regimes in areas of federal competence.

cons.claim: Produces overlapping regulation, forum-shopping, and recurring uncertainty about the scope of federal versus state authority.
cons.evidence: Long-running litigation over Commerce Clause and preemption illustrates boundary disputes.

jurisdictions.citation: U.S. Const. amends. X; structural provisions art. I–III

tenth-amendment-overview.title: Tenth Amendment — powers reserved to the states

federalism-boundary-tension.title: Federalism and overlapping jurisdiction — introductory note

data.name: Judicial review
data.description: Courts may assess whether statutes and executive actions comply with the Constitution and refuse to enforce those that do not—tying the written constitution to ordinary adjudication.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Long treated as settled in federal practice since early 19th-century precedent, though its scope and legitimacy remain debated in theory.

pros.claim: Gives bite to constitutional limits that might otherwise be ignored by political majorities.
pros.evidence: Invalidation of unconstitutional enactments is a routine part of federal and state court practice.

cons.claim: Places major policy outcomes in the hands of unelected judges, raising democratic legitimacy and restraint debates.
cons.evidence: Scholarly and popular controversy over countermajoritarian difficulty and interpretive methodology.

countermajoritarian-debate.title: Judicial review and democratic theory — introductory note

data.name: Rule of law
data.description: Government officials—including law enforcement and courts—are bound by law; powers are exercised through known rules and procedures rather than arbitrary will, supporting predictability and accountability.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Widely invoked across U.S. legal culture as an ideal, though its content is contested and partially enforced through many distinct doctrines.

pros.claim: Anchors legitimacy in public norms that constrain coercion and protect expectations.
pros.evidence: Constitutional limits, administrative procedure, and judicial review are often framed as rule-of-law mechanisms.

cons.claim: The phrase is capacious enough to be used rhetorically on opposing sides of the same dispute.
cons.evidence: Competing invocations in debates over discretion, emergencies, and enforcement priorities.

jurisdictions.citation: Cross-cutting theme; not a single clause

rule-of-law-ideal.title: Rule of law — basic elements (generality, stability, prospectivity)

rule-of-law-contested-use.title: Contested meanings of the rule of law in public debate

data.name: Separation of powers
data.description: Legislative, executive, and judicial functions are assigned to distinct branches at the federal level, with checks and balances intended to prevent concentrated power and arbitrary rule.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Explicit in Articles I–III; treated as a core structural principle in U.S. constitutional doctrine.

pros.claim: Reduces the risk that a single actor can make, enforce, and interpret law without accountability from other branches.
pros.evidence: Institutional design allocates distinct core functions and inter-branch checks.

cons.claim: Can slow decision-making and invite branch conflict, gridlock, or emergency-power stretching of formal lines.
cons.evidence: Recurring debates over war powers, appointments, and enforcement discretion illustrate friction.

articles-i-iii-structure.title: U.S. Constitution, Articles I–III (legislative, executive, judicial branches)

separation-friction-note.title: Separation of powers and inter-branch conflict — introductory note

data.name: Stare decisis (respect for precedent)
data.description: Courts generally follow prior decisions on the same legal question to promote stability, reliance, and equal treatment—while allowing rare departures when precedent is unworkable or egregiously wrong.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Strong norm in appellate practice, though the Supreme Court has articulated exceptions and occasionally overturns landmark precedents.

pros.claim: Supports predictability for individuals, institutions, and markets that order conduct around prior holdings.
pros.evidence: Routine lower-court adherence to controlling precedent is expected absent distinguishing facts.

cons.claim: Can entrench mistaken or morally outdated decisions until a court is willing to bear the costs of reversal.
cons.evidence: High-profile overrulings illustrate tension between stability and correction.

jurisdictions.citation: See e.g. Planned Parenthood of Se. Pa. v. Casey, 505 U.S. 833 (1992) (stare decisis factors)

stare-decisis-rationale.title: Stare decisis — institutional reliance and stability

data.name: US Right to Try Act
data.description: Federal law allowing terminally ill patients to access experimental treatments that have completed Phase I clinical trials but are not yet FDA-approved.
data.foundationStrengthRationale: Broadly supported across party lines; some concerns from FDA about safety oversight gaps.

pros.claim: Expands patient autonomy over their own medical decisions at end of life.
pros.evidence: Consistent with Cruzan v. Director, MDH (1990) establishing right to refuse treatment, logically extendable to right to pursue treatment.

pros.claim: Provides hope and options where none previously existed within the regulatory framework.
pros.evidence: Prior to the act, expanded access (compassionate use) required lengthy FDA review averaging 4+ months.

cons.claim: May expose vulnerable patients to ineffective or harmful treatments without adequate safety data.
cons.evidence: Phase I trials establish basic safety but not efficacy; only ~10% of Phase I drugs reach approval.

cons.claim: Could undermine clinical trial enrollment if patients can access drugs outside trials.
cons.evidence: Some researchers report difficulty recruiting for Phase II/III trials in therapeutic areas where Right to Try is active.

cruzan-v-missouri-1990.title: Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health
